pharm: Stimulates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction, raising systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure with reflex bradycardia
quick: IV bolus 40-100 mcg every 1-2 min (max 200 mcg/dose); infusion 10-35 mcg/min, max 200 mcg/min - titrate
Not applicable (IV injection); dilute before use
Used during Cesarean section; no established risk of birth defects at term
Limited data; short half-life - clinical effect on breastfed infant unlikely

No specific adjustment stated in injection labeling
Blood pressure, heart rate, IV site for extravasation, perfusion
summary: Phenylephrine hydrochloride injection is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist (vasopressor) indicated for the treatment of clinically important hypotension resulting primarily from vasodilation in the setting of anesthesia. It is diluted and given intravenously as a bolus or continuous infusion, titrated to the pressor response. Its effect is rapid and short-lived, and it characteristically causes reflex bradycardia as blood pressure rises.
indications: Treatment of clinically important hypotension resulting primarily from vasodilation in the setting of anesthesia

dosage.d: 40 mcg to 100 mcg IV every 1 to 2 minutes as needed
dosage.t: As needed, titrated to pressor response
dosage.n: Single bolus not to exceed 200 mcg; dilute before administration

dosage.d: 10 mcg/min to 35 mcg/min, titrate to effect
dosage.t: Continuous; adjust to blood pressure response
dosage.n: Infusion rate not to exceed 200 mcg/min; dilute in normal saline or 5% dextrose

admin: For intravenous administration only; must be diluted before use (10 mg/mL concentrate)
Bolus: dilute with normal saline or 5% dextrose in water to the desired concentration
Continuous infusion: dilute with normal saline or 5% dextrose in water
Inspect for particulate matter and discoloration; do not use if colored, cloudy or containing particulates
Titrate to the pressor (blood pressure) response; correct hypovolemia before/alongside use; avoid extravasation
moa: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist. Interaction with alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle causes vasoconstriction, increasing systolic and diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, and total peripheral vascular resistance. The pressor onset after an IV bolus is rapid (within minutes), and as blood pressure rises, vagal activity increases producing reflex bradycardia. It acts on most vascular beds including renal, pulmonary, and splanchnic arteries.

relative: Severe arteriosclerosis or history of angina (may precipitate angina)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (may increase pulmonary arterial pressure)
Concomitant MAO inhibitors or other agents that augment the pressor response
monitor: Blood pressure and heart rate continuously
IV site for extravasation; perfusion of extremities and vital organs

preg: Data from randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses of phenylephrine injection use in pregnant women during Cesarean section have not established a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, and have not identified adverse effects on maternal outcomes or infant Apgar scores. There are no data on use in the first or second trimester. Animal studies showed fetal malformations and decreased pup weights at multiples of the human daily dose.
lact: There is limited information on the presence of phenylephrine in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. Given its short half-life and parenteral use in the perioperative setting, a clinically important effect on a breastfed infant is unlikely; the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is described in the injection labeling; titrate to blood pressure response.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described in the injection labeling; titrate to blood pressure response.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) - markedly augment pressor effect, risk of hypertensive crisis
Oxytocin and oxytocic drugs - augment pressor effect
Ergot alkaloids (e.g. methylergonovine) - augment pressor effect
moderate: Atropine, steroids, norepinephrine transporter inhibitors (e.g. atomoxetine), angiotensin/aldosterone - increase pressor effect
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists, mixed alpha/beta antagonists - decrease pressor effect
PDE-5 inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, benzodiazepines, centrally acting sympatholytics - decrease pressor effect
interactions.diagnostics: Pressor and reflex-bradycardia effects may confound hemodynamic assessment

emergency: Severe hypertensive crisis with end-organ ischemia

monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm (reflex bradycardia, arrhythmia)
counsel: This medicine is given by injection or drip during anesthesia or in a monitored setting
Your blood pressure and heart rate will be watched closely
Tell your anesthetist/clinician about heart disease, angina, or any blood-pressure medicines you take
Report pain, swelling, or color change at the injection site immediately
pk: Rapid pressor effect within minutes of IV bolus
Blood-pressure rise within minutes of IV administration
Effective half-life ~5 minutes after infusion; terminal plasma elimination half-life ~2.5 hours
Short-lived pressor effect; metabolized by monoamine oxidase and sulfotransferase
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F), excursions 15-30 C; protect from light; diluted solution: <=4 h at room temp or <=24 h refrigerated
pearls: Pure alpha-1 agonist - raises blood pressure with reflex (vagally mediated) bradycardia, unlike norepinephrine
Useful vasopressor for anesthesia-induced hypotension and for spinal-anesthesia hypotension in Cesarean section
Always correct hypovolemia; phenylephrine treats vasodilatory, not hypovolemic, hypotension
Extravasation can cause tissue necrosis - phentolamine infiltration is the antidote
Avoid or use great caution with MAOIs and TCAs - risk of exaggerated hypertensive response
missed: Not applicable - phenylephrine injection is administered by a clinician by titration during anesthesia or critical care, not on a self-administered fixed schedule.
overdose: Overdose causes a rapid rise in blood pressure with headache, vomiting, a sensation of fullness in the head, tingling of the extremities, reflex bradycardia, and cardiac arrhythmias including ventricular extrasystoles and ventricular tachycardia. Management is to stop the infusion and provide supportive care; severe hypertension may be treated with an alpha-adrenergic blocker (e.g. phentolamine), and arrhythmias managed as clinically appropriate.
